Popular Safari extension StopTheMadness developer Jeff Johnson says that despite Apple's claims of reviewing submissions, blatant rating manipulation on the App Store has so far gone unnoticed.

He says that while he doesn't actively search for scam apps on the App Store, he often encounters them by chance, and shared a recent example...

App Store is a "safe and trusted place"

Apple has always taken a hard line against any antitrust measures involving third-party app stores or iPhone sideloading, only backing down when legally forced to. Even so, Apple continues to defend itself.

The company claims it does this not for money, but to protect iPhone users from malware. For instance, Apple said last year it had blocked over $9 billion in fraudulent transactions.

However, many developers are skeptical of the claim that "the App Store is a safe place," pointing to numerous scam cases involving millions of dollars. Just last month, Apple was sued by three customers who claimed their Bitcoin was entirely stolen by a fake wallet app.

App Store Rating Manipulation

App Store rating manipulation has been a long-standing problem, with companies even renting "iPhone farms" in mainland China to mass-download apps and leave five-star reviews.

Developer Jeff Johnson (best known for the StopTheMadness Safari extension) points out what he considers the latest "widespread and obvious" case of review fraud on the App Store. The app in question is TabControl Extension.

He says that when he stumbled upon this app, it was ranked 12th on the US Mac App Store paid Safari extensions chart, and featured a screenshot that was obviously AI-generated and fake.

Another notable point is that the fake screenshot claimed a "4.9 out of 5 stars" rating, leading people to believe these were ratings given by App Store users... Using App Store screenshots to make false claims is a common scam tactic I've mentioned before. When developers submit apps to the App Store, Apple reviews not only the app itself, but also the App Store listing data and metadata, including screenshots. The claims in scam app screenshots are often blatantly absurd, but Apple still approves them as a matter of course... Apple claims the App Store protects users from dishonest developers. If the App Store review can't even catch this kind of issue, what exactly is it doing? In fact, the App Store review doesn't need to investigate as deeply as I do. A screenshot claiming "4.9 out of 5 stars" is itself a red flag. Apple has all the rating and review records for every country, so they know perfectly well this is false advertising. I don't even need to download the damn app to know the developer is trying to deceive users.

As he puts it, if a developer is willing to use deceptive tactics to sell their app from the start, you certainly wouldn't want to hand over your browsing data to them.

9to5Mac's Take

Of course, eliminating all App Store scams is an impossible task, but fake reviews are extremely common, and cases like this one should be blatantly obvious to Apple. What's baffling is how this extension managed to pass review in the first place.

Apple should at least establish a mechanism to automatically conduct stricter reviews of any app that makes it onto any chart, examining both the app itself and the claims it makes.
